item.title: Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein September eNewsletter
item.description:
Sept. '23 - Protecting the Environment, Holding Corporations Accountable & More

From the Desk of City Attorney Zach Klein

As City Attorney, my priority has always been the health, safety and security of all those who live, work in or visit our city. From day one, we have leveraged the power of the City Attorney’s Office to put these priorities into action, filing proactive litigation to defend public safety, hold problem landlords accountable, and take on big corporations that abuse the trust of consumers and the public.   

In this newsletter, you can read about the work our office is doing to improve public health and safety in neighborhoods across the city, including:

  • Working with police and concerned neighbors to shut down a problem bar that’s been the scene of violent crime and multiple homicides in recent years;
  • Holding the landlords of an east side apartment complex accountable for living conditions so deplorable that tenants had to be evacuated. Working together, we were able to track these landlords down, take them to court, and get the property turned over to a responsible management team—all while ensuring tenants are in line to get the relief they deserve;
  • Filing a lawsuit against big chemical corporations that pollute our homes and environment with toxic “forever chemicals,” which can build up in the body over time and cause certain health issues. These chemicals are found in everyday household products and the environment, and the City is urging the Court to hold these companies accountable for the cleanup of these chemicals;
  • Taking the operators of a new west side bus terminal to court due to the substandard, unsanitary and unsafe conditions of the site, which have led to safety and security concerns for patrons and area neighbors since the terminal opened in June. The City is asking the operators to bring the site into compliance or find a more appropriate location to house their bus service;
  • Urging the Common Pleas Court to decide in favor of the ability for cities like Columbus to decide what public safety measures make sense for us, including commonsense ideas like ensuring firearms are stored safely out of the reach of children, limiting high capacity magazines often used in mass shootings, and making it easier for prosecutors to go after illegal gun sales.

It is a privilege to continue to serve as your City Attorney, and I encourage you to contact our office at any time to let us know your thoughts, concerns and more about the issues that matter most to you, your family, business or neighborhood. Please call 614.645.7385 or email CityAttorney@columbus.gov to share your thoughts on how we can better serve you.

City Attorney Zach Klein Files Lawsuit against North Columbus Bar Plagued by Violence and Crime

City Attorney Klein recently announced that the City of Columbus filed a complaint against the owners of Jack’s Corner Pub, a bar located at 2480 Summit Street north of the Ohio State campus. The bar has seen dozens of police runs and calls for service over the past two years, including multiple incidents of shots fired, fights, overdoses, theft and two homicides. The City is asking the Court to declare the bar a public nuisance and order owners to shut down the bar permanently.

“We want Columbus to have a vibrant, thriving nightlife, but it needs to be safe for patrons, workers and neighbors. The violence and crime we’re seeing at this bar is unacceptable, and for the safety of patrons, employees and the surrounding neighborhood, we may have no choice other than going to the Court and asking that this bar be shut down for good,” said Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein. “We appreciate the patience of the public as we’ve worked to build a strong case we believe will be successful before the Court so that we can end the chaos and improve public safety.”

According to court documents, Jack’s has seen 38 calls for service and complaints to CPD over the past two years, including for a reported homicide in March 2022 and repeated reports of shots fired, brawls erupting both inside and outside the establishment, overdoses, vehicle theft.

On July 28, 2023, a number of suspects were involved in a fight at the premises, which saw one suspect obtain a firearm and shoot an individual multiple times. The victim was pronounced dead at the scene.

The City’s lawsuit calls on the Court to declare Jack’s a public nuisance, require any current or future ownership groups to comply with all liquor laws and future court orders surrounding operations at the premises, including any potential limits on days and hours of operation or liquor sales. The City also reserves the right to ask the Court to permanently close the establishment or file a liquor license renewal objection.

City Attorney Zach Klein Statement as New Jersey Court Dismisses Latitude Five25 Ownership’s Bankruptcy Claim

City Attorney Klein issued a statement recently as the U.S. Bankruptcy Court District of New Jersey dismissed the bankruptcy claim made by Paxe Latitude, owners of the Latitude Five25 apartments on the east side of Columbus plagued my mismanagement and deplorable living conditions which have made the towers uninhabitable since Christmas Day 2022.

The decision now greenlights the takeover of the property by a receivership group to fix up the property and includes a $1.5 million settlement for former tenants of Latitude Five25. In addition, all involved parties, including tenants and the City, are able to pursue the full amount of the more than $4.3 million in contempt fines handed down by the Environmental Court in February.

Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein’s statement is below:

“The Court’s dismissal of this bankruptcy claim is a significant win for tenants and the City. A receivership group can now come in to take control over the property. Former tenants will finally see relief. The City is now free to go after the owners to recover the costs incurred by the City due to their gross mismanagement and negligence.

“This decision checks all the boxes we set out for when we decided to track these owners all the way to New Jersey, and delivers on our top priority: to ensure tenants have a fair settlement that puts money back in their pockets and ensure this ownership group hands over their keys so that a responsible management group can come in and make necessary repairs and investments in the property.

“This decision should send a message to any problem landlord in our City. If you don’t live up to your obligations as a landlord, we will use every legal tool we have to hold you accountable, whether here in Columbus or halfway across the country.”

City of Columbus Files Lawsuit to Hold Companies Accountable for Toxic “Forever Chemical” Production Linked to Contamination

City Attorney Klein announced recently that the City of Columbus filed a lawsuit against several major chemical companies for their negligence in the production of synthetic per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS), also known as “forever chemicals” due to components in them which break down very slowly. PFAS, which are present in many everyday household items and in the environment, can build up in the body over time and cause certain health problems. 

The City’s lawsuit, filed in the U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina, joins hundreds of other complaints made by cities across the country who are trying to hold these same companies accountable for the harm they have caused to the environment and risk to public health. In the complaint, the City is asking the Court to order companies to pay for environmental cleanup, including funds for future technology upgrades to ensure the City’s water supply remains safe and meets EPA standards.

“When corporations dumped toxic waste and pollution into our waterways and air, the government stepped in as a check, enacting EPA regulations to clean up our environment. Now, as companies contaminate our homes and environment with forever chemicals, it’s incumbent on government to step in again to protect the public and hold these corporations accountable for the damage they’ve caused. Companies like 3M and DuPont made this mess and they need to be the ones on the hook for cleaning it up,” said Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein.

According to the City’s complaint, numerous companies like 3M and DuPont produced forever chemicals knowing the toxicity of the products, which contaminated both the environment and homes of millions of Ohioans despite readily available technology to produce alternative products without the use of PFAS chemicals. The City also argues that the corporations failed to warn consumers and the public about the dangerous products, thereby threatening public health and safety.

The City’s lawsuit asks the Court to recover the substantial costs necessary to address any environmental contamination and protect the City’s drinking water supply from toxic forever chemicals, as well as punitive damages and other penalties associated with fraudulent and dangerous business practices the companies used to conceal and profit from the production of toxic forever chemicals.

Research shows that the vast majority of forever chemical exposure comes from air, foods, incidental ingestion and household products, such as nonstick cookware, stain resistant furniture and carpets, wrinkle free and water-repellent clothing, cosmetics, lubricants, paint, pizza boxes, popcorn bags, and many other products including firefighting foams that have been produced for decades by the corporations named in the lawsuit. Over time, exposure to these chemicals have been linked to numerous health issues, including high cholesterol, high blood pressure, fertility issues and certain types of cancers.

While a smaller percentage of PFAS exposure comes from water contamination, the City of Columbus Department of Public Utilities quality assurance lab technicians closely monitor the City’s water supply to ensure that it meets or exceeds all federal drinking water standards. City officials say that continued production and use of forever chemicals may require the installation of additional technology to maintain chemical levels in line with EPA standards, a cost which the City believes needs to be borne by the corporations named in the lawsuit.

City of Columbus Seeks Preliminary Injunction against Owners of West Side Bus Terminal for Failing to Address Concerns over Safety, Security and Sanitation

City Attorney Klein recently announced that the City of Columbus filed a lawsuit seeking a preliminary injunction against Barons Bus Incorporated, the owners of the property located at 845 N. Wilson Rd. that currently operates as a bus terminal for Barons and Greyhound bus lines. Since opening in June, the west side terminal has been plagued by safety, security and sanitation concerns, and in July, City officials gave operators notice of violations and a timeline to address the issues.

With the timeline now passed, City Attorney Klein is taking legal action to hold Barons accountable by urging the Court to declare the property a public nuisance and order owners to bring the property into compliance or move.

“Moving a business from one location to another doesn’t give owners permission to operate a public nuisance at the expense of the surrounding neighborhoods. The City will hold bus line operators to the same standards no matter where they do business,” said Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein.

“Public safety is our priority and the amount of crime at the terminal and the conditions which patrons are subjected to are unacceptable. The City Attorney’s Office will use every legal tool we have to ensure that any bus line operator in Columbus is safe, accessible and compliant—just like we did when we took Greyhound to court in 2021. These companies need to make significant improvements immediately or find a new location for their terminal.”

According to the City’s complaint, the property remains in violation of the City Building Code as no certificate for occupancy has been issued for the site’s current use as a major bus terminal. Additionally, City officials noted a number of safety and sanitation issues, including overcrowded waiting areas, unauthorized portable restroom facilities, inadequate loading and unloading zones, among other violations.

The City’s complaint also noted concerns about increased criminal activity in and around the terminal, which has seen a sharp increase in police calls for service since opening several months ago. In the six weeks prior to Defendants beginning operations, Columbus Police were called to the premises, or to neighboring properties for conduct related to the premises, approximately 30 times and took only one criminal offense report. In the six weeks after Defendants began operations, Columbus Police were called to the premises, or to neighboring properties for conduct related to the premises, approximately 62 times and took 14 criminal offense reports.  The calls for service include complaints for assault, robbery, shots fired and disturbances.

The City is asking the Court for a preliminary injunction against owners and to declare the property a public nuisance and order Barons to bring the property into compliance with all applicable codes or face potential closure.

City Attorney Zach Klein Files Motion for Judgment in Lawsuit Challenging State Restrictions on Local Gun Safety Measures

City Attorney Klein recently announced that the City of Columbus has filed a motion for summary judgement in its ongoing lawsuit challenging a state law prohibiting local communities from passing any gun-related safety measures, including commonsense ideas that the vast majority of Ohioans support like safe storage laws. The 10th District Court of Appeals recently sent the case back to the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas to resume proceedings in the case.

The City won a preliminary judgement in late 2022 and passed a number of gun safety measures, which have been on hold for a number of months as the State and NRA-backed groups challenged the ordinances in court.

A statement from Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein is below:

“We are seeking a ruling in our favor so that we can get back to doing the People’s work—enacting and enforcing commonsense measures that allow police and prosecutors to do their jobs and keep our kids and communities safe.

“The City is ready to defend its right to decide what laws make sense for us here at the local level as we do our part to curb gun violence, get weapons out of the hands of individuals who have no regard for human lives or the rule of law, and improve public safety.

“Every day that we’re blocked from enforcing safe storage or other commonsense laws on the books makes our neighborhoods and communities less safe. Residents are calling on us to do something to address gun violence. The law and the public are on our side, and we look forward to making our case to the Court so that we can give police and prosecutors the tools they need to uphold the law and hold accountable those who threaten public health and safety.”

August 2023 - Innovative Program to Decrease Retail Theft, Protecting Public Safety & More

From the Desk of City Attorney Zach Klein

As your City Attorney, my priority is you, the residents, small business owners, workers and everyone who calls Columbus home. It’s my job to listen to you about the issues that matter most in our neighborhoods, from public safety and crime to cleaning up blighted properties and connecting people to the tools they need to live a better life.

I believe that as an elected official, when the people speak, we must listen. That’s why earlier this month I spoke out in opposition to Issue 1, the ballot measure that would have upended citizen-led initiatives as we know them and fundamentally shifted the balance of power in our democracy away from the people.

When the returns started to come in, I quickly saw that Ohioans agreed. Up and down the state, voters spoke loudly and clearly, soundly defeating the brazen attempt to undermine their ability to hold an extreme legislature in check at the ballot box. They understood that Issue 1 was a fringe idea outside the bounds of representative government. On Election Night, the fringe lost and democracy won. Majority rule, and the power to shape the future of our city and state, remains with the people.

The results of this election reaffirm what we all hold true, that good government is only possible when the needs of the people—not those in power or the ones who fund their campaigns—come first. That’s why the City Attorney’s Office continues to crack down on violent crime, defend our ability to come together as a City to demand commonsense gun safety laws, and clean up problem properties that make us all less safe. In recent weeks, we’ve taken on hate and bias crimes, announced an innovative program to better lives and reduce retail theft, and fought back against the State and NRA-backed groups trying to do everything in their power to limit us from enacting and enforcing laws to keep our kids and communities safe.

It is a privilege to serve as your City Attorney, and I encourage you to contact our office at any time to let us know your thoughts, concerns and the issues that matter most to you, your family, business or neighborhood. Please call 614.645.7385 or email CityAttorney@columbus.gov to share your thoughts on how we can better serve you.

City Attorney Klein Commends High Bond in Domestic Violence Case Where Abuser Threatened Infant and Mother with Firearm, Attacked Police Officer

City Attorney Klein recently commended Franklin County Municipal Court Judge Andrea C. Peeples for issuing a $500,000 bond in a domestic violence case where the defendant assaulted his girlfriend, discharged a weapon, threatened to shoot the victim and their infant child, and assaulted a responding Columbus Police (CPD) Officer. The offender has been charged with multiple misdemeanor offenses, including domestic violence, assault, endangering children and aggravated menacing, as well as a felony harassment with a body substance count for biting the responding officer.

“The criminal justice system exists not just to prosecute violent individuals, but to protect victims and their families. Making it harder for the most dangerous offenders to get out and commit further, more lethal acts of violence remains a priority. This is especially important in domestic violence cases,” said Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein. “I continue to urge our judges to do their part to grant higher bonds and stricter requirements so that we can protect victims and save lives.”

Judge Peeples’ bond decision comes as City Attorney Klein and Prosecutors continue to push for higher cash bonds for violent domestic abusers who pose a significant threat to victims and their families. Since May, prosecutors have asked for a minimum $500,000 cash surety bond for domestic violence offenses involving a firearm or significant bodily injury to the victim, as well as requests for GPS monitoring, no use of alcohol or drugs with random drug screenings, and no weapons possession for the duration of the case for offenders. 

Domestic violence-related homicides are on the rise across the country, and the number of these homicides in the City of Columbus this year have already surpassed the total number that occurred in 2022, an alarming surge city officials hope to curb with these changes.

“I’m encouraged by the judge’s bond decision and hopeful that more judges give these higher bonds to keep violent offenders off the streets and more closely monitor their actions upon release,” said Melanie Tobias, the City Attorney’s Deputy Chief of Staff, Prosecution Division.

According to court documents, as Columbus Police were responding to a call in the 900 block of Higbee Drive South, an officer heard an individual calling for help. The officer then saw the victim being assaulted by the defendant, who had twisted the victim’s arm behind her back and appeared to be striking her from behind. The victim was holding their infant child.

Earlier in the night, the defendant had threatened to shoot both the victim and child and blocked the victim from getting into a vehicle to flee his control. As the responding officer attempted to place the defendant under arrest, he resisted, bit the officer on the arm, and remained aggressive and violent, yelling that he wanted officers to shoot him.

If convicted, the offender could face up to a year in prison and/or $2,500 fine for the felony charge and a maximum of 180 days in jail and $1,000 fine for misdemeanor offenses.

Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein Announces Hate Crime Charges in Two Separate Ethnic Intimidation Cases

Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein recently announced that City Prosecutors charged two individuals with misdemeanor ethnic intimidation charges stemming from separate hate crime incidents in Columbus. If convicted, the defendants could face up to 180 days jail and up to a $1,000 fine for their alleged bias crimes along with other penalties for additional charges. The cases come as the number of reported hate crimes continues to rise across the country.

“In Columbus, we welcome and celebrate our diverse heritage of cultures, religions and backgrounds. Hate has no place here. Those who terrorize our neighbors with acts of hate and senseless violence will be prosecuted to the fullest extent possible under the law. Holding these criminals accountable remains a top priority,” said Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein.

In June 2023, one of the charged defendants entered a gas station on W. 5th Ave. in Columbus, where he approached the register and began to yell anti-Muslim epithets at a store employee. Following the brief verbal tirade, the defendant then rushed behind the counter and attacked the victim, striking him multiple times with what appeared to be a knife or screwdriver. The story was corroborated by at least one witness, who along with another patron of the store came to the aid of the victim by pulling the defendant away from the victim. The defendant in this case has been charged with one count of assault and one count of ethnic intimidation from the incident.

The other case charged this week stems from an April 2022 incident where that defendant threatened his neighbor and repeatedly yelled racial slurs and anti-immigrant epithets at the victim. The defendant approached the victim wearing boxing gloves and brandishing a metal baton, where he proceeded to threaten the victim, chase him around his car and yell obscenities at him. The account was corroborated by three witnesses. The offender in this case has been charged with one count of ethnic intimidation and one count of menacing.

“Going after criminals who commit acts of hate and violence is our top priority and a grave matter of public safety,” said Joseph Gibson, the City’s Chief Prosecutor. “Thanks to CPD and the FBI who investigated these incidents and the witnesses who came forward to help us hold these offenders accountable for their deplorable actions.”

City Attorney Klein Announces Court Orders Shutting Down Pair of West Side Drug Houses

Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein announced in July that the City of Columbus took legal action to shut down two drug houses on the city’s west side, securing preliminary injunctions in the Franklin County Municipal Court’s Environmental Division to shutter several properties known for drugs and violent crime. CPD then executed court orders to board up the properties located at 451 Josephine Ave. in the Hilltop neighborhood and 112 S. Cypress Ave. in Franklinton.

“The City continues to prioritize cracking down on problem properties where criminals push deadly drugs into our streets and attract chaos and violence,” said Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein. “No parent, child or resident should have to worry about which houses or neighborhood blocks to avoid as they wait for the bus, send their kids to school, or go about their day. Our west side neighborhoods are stronger with these dangerous properties contained and those who threaten public safety held accountable.”

According to court documents, CPD responded to multiple domestic disturbances related to threats of violence at the Josephine Ave. property in 2022. In November 2022, CPD received a call that a tenant at the premises had turned the property into a drug house.

In May 2023, CPD received complaints of a drug deal at the premises as well as multiple reports of shots fired. Later in May, CPD received a complaint of suspected narcotics use at the premises, responded to the property on reports of a stolen vehicle, and were dispatched after receiving reports of an overdose on site.

The Franklinton property, located at 112 S. Cypress Ave., came to the attention of CPD in March 2023 when a concerned neighbor reported suspicious behavior at the premises. In April 2023, CPD received a complaint from an individual claiming to have entered the property to purchase drugs, but that a property resident pulled a gun on him and forced him to leave the premises.

In May 2023, CPD conducted multiple controlled purchases of crack cocaine and fentanyl from the premises. Later that month, CPD detectives obtained and executed a search warrant at the premises, where officers recovered crack cocaine, cocaine, two semi-automatic handguns, various magazines and ammunition, and stolen property.

In June 2023, CPD responded to multiple reports of burglaries in progress at the premises and other disturbances on the property. 

“Residents, families and business owners in Franklinton, the Hilltop and every Columbus neighborhood deserve a safe place to live, work, raise a family and operate a business,” said Assistant City Attorney Zach Gwin, the City’s lead attorney responding to problem properties in west side neighborhoods. “By getting these drug houses off line and the criminals who prey on our streets behind bars, we can lift up neighborhoods one property and block at a time, building better, safer communities for all of us.”

City Attorney Klein Highlights Innovative Program to Decrease Retail Theft, Improve Public Safety and Help Businesses Thrive

City Attorney Zach Klein announced that the City of Columbus has been selected as one of five sites nationwide to pilot a low-level retail theft intervention project by the Association of Prosecuting Attorneys (APA), in partnership with Justice System Partners (JSP). Low-level retail theft, which refers to smaller-scale, lower-value shoplifting incidents, has risen in recent years, harming retailers who have been impacted by shrinkage and leading to an increase in arrests.

Columbus’ program, known as Buckeye Deflection, works through the City Attorney’s Prosecution Division to identify low-level offenders whose crimes stem from certain underlying factors, such as unmet mental health needs, substance use and/or co-occurring disorders, or housing or food insecurity. These quality-of-life issues disproportionately affect low-income households and persons of color, which can exacerbate racial and ethnic disparities when these individuals come into contact with the criminal justice system. The aim of the program is to connect these individuals with community resources to improve their quality of life and prevent future theft. While some individuals may still face prosecution for their offenses, every individual is given access to the help they need.

“Buckeye Deflection is working to improve lives and meet the needs of those struggling in our community while also freeing up prosecutors to go after violent and higher level criminals who pose a serious threat to public safety,” said Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein. “Businesses are on board with Buckeye Deflection because they know that when individuals have access to the tools they need to live a better life, theft decreases and business improves. I look forward to working with the APA to expand our innovative program to transform lives and further reduce crime in neighborhoods across Columbus.”

Buckeye Deflection is the next iteration of City Attorney Klein’s already successful Buckeye Diversion program. Through the nationally recognized and first-of-its-kind Buckeye Diversion program, participants are assessed and given individual plans to get their lives on track and turn away from crime. Like Buckeye Diversion, admission to Buckeye Deflection is determined on a case by case basis, and those engaged in violent crime, higher level theft and continued, repeat offenses will not qualify for the program and will continue to be prosecuted.

Since its inception in 2019, the Buckeye Diversion Program has impacted the lives of 248 individuals. In 2023, the program has seen 24 successful completions with another 64 participants currently enrolled in the program. Nearly 80 percent of those who completed a Buckeye Diversion program have not reoffended.

“While City prosecutors continue to crack down on criminals who have no regard for the law or the harm they cause small businesses, there is a small subset of individuals engaged in low-level retail theft whose actions stem from unmet needs like homelessness, mental health disorders or food insecurity,” said Jennifer Grant, who leads the Columbus Buckeye Deflection Program. “Buckeye Deflection gives us the tools to better identify these individuals and connect them with the critical resources they need rather than throwing them into a cycle of incarceration and reoffending. The data we’re seeing shows that this program works and helps the bottom line of our business partners.”

Columbus participated in a competitive RFP process and was selected from applications received from prosecutors’ offices nationwide. The City will work with APA and JSP to expand Buckeye Deflection to be able to better identify and address the needs of those who commit low-level retail theft and improve public safety by working directly with retailers and the communities they serve.

item.title: Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein eNewsletter
item.description:
July 2023 - Fighting Crime, Gun Safety Laws, Supreme Court Rulings & More

From the Desk of City Attorney Zach Klein

As your City Attorney, I am focused on fighting every day for the people who live, work, visit, go to school, raise a family and operate a business right here in Columbus. Your rights and safety are my top priority.

The City Attorney’s Office continues to crack down on violent crime and those whose actions threaten public safety, harm local businesses and disrupt the peace in neighborhoods across the city. Additionally, we’re committed to defending the rights of cities like Columbus who want to take real, meaningful action on gun safety measures that make a difference in our communities, from safe storage requirements to making it easier for police and prosecutors to do their jobs to get illegal firearms off our streets and put the criminals who sell and possess these weapons behind bars.

In this newsletter, you can read about:

  • The U.S. Supreme Court’s most recent rulings that threaten to set us back on a number of fronts, and the importance of continuing to fight for the issues that matter most to our community.
  • The City’s recent crackdown on criminals engaged in street takeovers that threaten public safety and hurt local businesses. This lawless behavior is unacceptable in any neighborhood, and City prosecutors are taking a hard line to hold these offenders accountable.
  • The important role safe storage laws play in eliminating accidental shooting injuries and deaths of minors.
  • The City’s continued fight to enact and enforce commonsense gun safety laws that respect the Second Amendment, encourage responsible gun ownership, and hold accountable those whose actions threaten the health and safety of our children and the public.

It is a privilege to serve as your City Attorney, and I will continue to listen to your thoughts and concerns about the issues that matter most to you, your family and your neighborhood or business. I encourage you to contact our office at any time to let us know about what’s important to you. Please call 614.645.7385 or email CityAttorney@columbus.gov to share your thoughts on how we can better serve you.

City Attorney Zach Klein Statement on Latest Supreme Court Rulings

City Attorney Klein issued a statement regarding several high profile U.S. Supreme Court rulings that will have broad, sweeping implications for millions of Americans, from decisions gutting affirmative action policies and permitting discrimination against LGBTQ+ individuals to scrapping President Biden’s student loan relief plan. Klein also spoke out on a case set to come before the Court in the next term regarding laws prohibiting domestic abusers from possessing firearms.

“In the final days of the term, this Court took several unprecedented, wrongheaded actions that will have real world implications for millions of Americans, from striking down affirmative action and President Biden’s student debt plan to giving a green light to any business that wants to discriminate against LGBTQ+ individuals.

“Make no mistake, these short-sighted, politically-motivated decisions will harm Americans and set us back in our march toward a nation and society that values justice, fairness, and equality not just for some of us, but for all of us.

“And while we now must chart a different path forward in the fight for racial equity, non-discrimination protections and debt relief, we must also keep our eyes focused on what comes next before this radical Court, including a case that will have far reaching consequences for victims of domestic violence and the ability of their abusers to access dangerous and deadly weapons.

“Despite the Court’s repeated blows to progress and precedent, the fight doesn’t end here. There’s more work to do, more cases to argue, and more battles to wage as we work to improve lives, deliver on the promise of good government, and expand opportunity and justice for every American.”

City Attorney Klein Announces Criminal Charges against Group Involved in Gas Station Takeover

Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein announced charges have been filed against nine adults stemming from a street takeover event in May 2023 where a group overran a gas station in Northeast Columbus, blocked traffic and access to the lot, and engaged in theft of merchandise from the premises.

In addition to the nine individuals charged with misdemeanor theft by City Prosecutors, 10 juveniles have been referred for prosecution within the Franklin County juvenile court system.

City Attorney Klein is instructing prosecutors handling the City’s cases not to offer any plea deals and push for one hundred percent of fines and penalties for offenders.

“People are tired of the chaos and lawlessness of a small group of individuals who think the law doesn’t apply to them. This behavior harms businesses and threatens public safety and it won’t be tolerated anywhere in Columbus. That’s why, in partnership with CPD, the City is cracking down and prosecuting these cases to the fullest extent possible under the law. We want to send a message that if you engage in this lawless behavior, you’re going to eat one hundred percent of fines and penalties,” said City Attorney Zach Klein.

Last summer, the City unveiled Operation Wheels Down to crack down on the illegal, reckless operation of ATVs, motorbikes and other vehicles on city streets, leading to numerous vehicles impounded and dozens of individuals charged and prosecuted to the fullest extent.

This year, CPD’s Operation Burnout, which has focused on street takeover events, reckless driving and other related crimes, has led to hundreds of citations, dozens of arrests and more than 100 vehicles impounded as part of the operation.

“I would like to thank our community partners who provided information leading to the identification of the people involved in these crimes. Additionally, Columbus Police Detectives worked collaboratively with the community and the City Attorney’s Office to appropriately charge those involved in these criminal acts. Taking over streets, victimizing businesses and endangering the people of Columbus is unacceptable. We appreciate the support of City Attorney Zach Klein and his entire staff for their thorough prosecution of these criminal cases,” said Columbus Division of Police Assistant Chief Greg Bodker.

The City noted that if any other evidence from this incident is brought to light, further charges could be filed to hold the identified individuals accountable for additional offenses.

Scientific Study Finds Nearly All Accidental Shootings by Minors Are Preventable with Safe Storage Laws

Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein issued a statement in response to a new study conducted by the Center for Injury Research and Policy at Columbus’ Nationwide Children’s Hospital, which found that 92 percent of accidental shootings involving a minor happened when a gun was stored unlocked and loaded either in the child’s own home or that of a friend. Preliminary results from research conducted by the Ohio Department of Health suggest that the majority of Ohioans who keep loaded firearms in the home do not lock their weapons.

“We’ve seen the videos and heard the horror stories of children finding and discharging a loaded firearm in the home, injuring or killing themselves or others. Just this past week, we saw an Ohio toddler pick up a gun and accidentally shoot his pregnant mother, killing both her and the fetus.

“Now, a study conducted by Nationwide Children’s Hospital researchers confirms what we’ve known for a long time—nearly all accidental shootings involving minors are preventable with safe storage. That’s why it is so important that the City continues to educate the public about the importance of safe storage and to defend our right to enact commonsense requirements that the vast majority of parents and gun owners support.

“We need to make it easier for police and prosecutors to do their job, protect our children, and hold irresponsible gun owners accountable when their negligence threatens our kids’ lives. That begins with the State joining our efforts on safe storage or getting out of the way to let us do what they’ve failed to do for decades: keep our kids and communities safe.”

The City of Columbus filed a lawsuit against the State of Ohio challenging its gun pre-emption law in 2019, won a preliminary judgement on the case in November 2022, and enacted several commonsense gun safety ordinances in December 2022, including legislation requiring gun owners to lock and safely store their firearms in the home so that they are inaccessible to minors.

City Attorney Klein announced the City’s first safe storage prosecution in April 2023 in a case where a child of the defendant found an unlocked and loaded gun in a couch cushion, pointed the weapon toward his face, and accidentally discharged the weapon, narrowly missing his head.

However, due to ongoing litigation brought by the State of Ohio and NRA-backed groups, several of the City’s gun ordinances are on hold, which is preventing police and prosecutors from filing charges in several cases where the City’s new safe storage statute could be applied.

City of Columbus Defends Its Right to Enact and Enforce Safe Storage and Other Gun Laws

Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein recently issued a statement as the City presented its arguments before the 10th District Court of Appeals in the State of Ohio’s appeal of a decision by a Franklin County judge to temporarily halt a state law that prohibits cities like Columbus from enacting and enforcing gun safety ordinances.

As a result of the City’s victory in Franklin County in November 2022 that opened the door for legislative action on gun safety, Columbus City Council passed a number of gun safety ordinances in December 2022, including safe storage requirements to keep firearms out of the hands of minors, bans on high capacity magazines commonly used in mass shootings, and a provision to make it easier for police and prosecutors to target illegal guns on the streets.

“Recklessly passing legislation at the Statehouse to pour limitless guns into our streets with no checks and no training has led to chaos and needless death, but the State continues to stand in the way of the ability for cities like Columbus to do anything about it,” said Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein. “The City of Columbus will continue to defend its right to enact laws that protect public safety, keep our kids and communities safe, and support police and prosecutors to do their jobs to enforce the laws already on the books and keep guns out of the wrong hands.”

In April 2023, City Attorney Klein announced the City’s first prosecution under its new safe storage law, which involved a case where a child of the defendant accessed and discharged a firearm owned by the defendant, which nearly struck the child, causing burns and short term hearing loss as another child looked on.

“Safe storage saves lives. We all watched in horror at the video of the young child pulling a firearm from beneath a couch cushion, pointing it toward his head, and pulling the trigger, narrowly missing the child’s face. Because of our safe storage law, that parent is facing the consequences. But now, the State and NRA-backed groups are standing in the way of other children and families faced with the same situation,” added City Attorney Klein.

Enforcement of the City’s safe storage law is currently on hold following a flurry of additional lawsuits filed by the State of Ohio and NRA-backed groups challenging the City’s gun ordinances. As such, a number of safe storage cases remain uncharged, limiting the ability of police and prosecutors to do their jobs to enforce the law and seek justice for children and families affected by irresponsible gun owners.

“The State’s push for more guns and less oversight has predictably led to more violence and preventable tragedies. The City of Columbus will continue to defend its right to decide what kind of gun safety measures work best for us,” said Columbus Solicitor General Rich Coglianese, the City’s lead attorney in the case challenging the state’s gun pre-emption laws. “It’s our hope that the 10th District rules favorably so that police and prosecutors can get back to enforcing the laws and keeping our kids and communities safe.”

June 2023 - Addressing Gun Violence, Protecting Victims & More

From the Desk of City Attorney Zach Klein

As City Attorney, the safety of all who live, work in or visit our city is always a top priority, whether it’s in our neighborhoods, at summer festivals and events, or public spaces all across Columbus. The City Attorney’s Office regularly works alongside our friends in law enforcement, health and safety personnel, and community leaders to address public safety concerns, improve conditions for residents and businesses, and keep Columbus a vibrant, thriving city for all of us.

In recent weeks, much focus has gone into ensuring safety in entertainment districts, improving security at nuisance bars, cracking down on street takeovers and all forms of reckless driving on our city’s streets, and working to reduce gun violence wherever it threatens lives and livelihoods. As the calendar turns to summer, the City Attorney’s Office is committed to going above and beyond to promote public safety and hold dangerous, violent individuals accountable for the threats they pose to our community by getting them off the streets and putting them behind bars.

In this newsletter, you can read about:

  • The City’s ongoing efforts to reduce gun violence and improve public safety in high density areas like entertainment districts, parks, and large-scale sporting events and festivals.
  • How the City Attorney’s Office is speaking out against proposed state legislation that would make it easier for convicted domestic abusers to access concealed weapons.
  • How the City is stepping in to improve safety and security at a bar in the Hilltop that has a history of gun violence.
  • The City Attorney’s Office’s opposition to a recently-passed resolution that would make it harder for Ohio voters to amend our constitution.

It is a privilege to serve as your City Attorney, and I will continue to listen to your thoughts and concerns about the issues that matter most to you, your family and your neighborhood or business. I encourage you to contact our office at any time to let us know about what’s important to you. Please call 614.645.7385 or email CityAttorney@columbus.gov to share your thoughts on how we can better serve you.

As City Leaders Push for Safer Streets, City Attorney Klein Files Lawsuit to Expand City’s Ability to Take Meaningful Action on Gun Safety

When City leaders recently gathered in the Short North to outline a multi-pronged neighborhood safety strategy, City Attorney Klein announced his office has filed a lawsuit that would allow law enforcement and prosecutors to enforce gun safety measures that are already on the books and let the City take additional actions to improve public safety in entertainment districts, parks and other high traffic, densely populated areas of the city.

The City’s lawsuit against the State of Ohio, filed in the Franklin County Court of Common Pleas, would urge the Court to declare that the City’s gun safety ordinances, including requirements for safe storage of firearms, prohibitions on high-capacity magazines, and measures to make it easier to prosecute individuals selling guns to dangerous criminals prohibited from possessing firearms, are enforceable and that the state law restricting local authority on commonsense gun laws is unconstitutional, as was preliminarily ruled on by the Court in November 2022.

“We know what it takes to make our neighborhoods safe: police, prosecution, people, and the political will to enact effective gun laws. Here in Columbus, we’re investing in these things and enacting the kinds of laws that will make a difference, but state officials continue to intentionally make it harder for police to do their job and for the City to take the actions we know will promote responsible gun ownership and reduce gun violence in our neighborhoods—the actions people in neighborhoods from the Short North to Linden are asking for,” said Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein. 

The lawsuit comes amid much confusion as opponents, including the State of Ohio, continue an all-out assault on the City’s attempts to enforce safety measures meant to reduce gun violence and keep kids and communities safe. Lawsuits have been filed in multiple counties to block the implementation of the City’s gun safety ordinances. In one lawsuit, state officials have used arguments that go so far as to say that a City ordinance keeping firearms out of the hands of minors is unconstitutional because Ohio allowed for child soldiers during the Civil War.

If the Court strikes down the State’s prohibition on even the most minor local gun safety ordinances, City Attorney Klein says that could open the door for real conversations on how best to reduce gun violence, encourage responsible gun ownership, and deploy safety strategies that would work best in Columbus, including implementing gun free zones in entertainment districts like the Short North, city parks and other community events with large crowds like festivals, parades and sporting events.

“Entertainment districts like the Short North, parks or areas around arenas or stadiums on game days where there is a mix of alcohol, heavy traffic and high volumes of people aren’t places where we need more guns, but state restrictions are making it harder for police to do their jobs and for the City to ensure safety for all who live, work and visit these areas,” added Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein.

The lawsuit also challenges a state law passed in 2022 that puts burdensome prohibitions on local authorities from declaring emergencies that would require the temporary closure of businesses in a given area to protect the health and safety of the community, including gun stores. The City argues that this prohibition could threaten public safety during a state of emergency.

“The City is prepared to defend its right to enact and enforce gun safety laws that make sense for us here in Columbus, just as we are in countless other areas of the law,” said Columbus Solicitor General Rich Coglianese. “Carving out exceptions because that’s what the NRA wants doesn’t make it constitutional. It simply makes it harder for police and prosecutors to do their jobs.”

In April, City Attorney Klein announced a guilty plea in the first test of the City’s safe storage law on a case where a young child found a loaded gun in between couch cushions, picked the firearm up to play with it, pointed it toward his head, and accidentally discharged the weapon.

City officials have pointed to several similar incidents in recent weeks where minors have discharged weapons, but because of the State’s court action to temporarily halt the City’s gun safety ordinances, no charges for safe storage violations can be made at the current time even if the facts of the case show a clear violation of the City’s ordinance, making it harder for police and prosecutors to hold accountable those responsible for minors accessing these firearms.

City Attorney Zach Klein Testifies Against Bill that Would Give Convicted Domestic Abusers Access to Concealed Weapons

Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein submitted testimony to the Ohio House Government Oversight Committee in opposition to the Gun Violence Expansion Act, House Bill 51, legislation that would expand free access to firearms in Ohio, including for individuals convicted of certain domestic violence offenses, and make it harder for police to enforce laws that are already on the books.

“As City Attorney, my priority is public safety, and this bill is a step in the wrong direction that makes us all less safe. It will put more guns in the hands of violent domestic abusers to use to torment their victims and make it harder for law enforcement to work together to crack down on the worst of the worst criminals,” said Columbus City Attorney Klein. “The chaos and havoc of gun violence in our city is exacerbated by really bad laws like this one. Passing laws like HB 51 only makes gun violence worse. Anyone who cares about public safety and addressing the scourge of gun crimes and domestic violence should be concerned about HB 51.”

HB 51 proposes to amend Ohio’s definition of who is allowed to carry a concealed weapon by removing federal disqualifying language. This means that only individuals who are prohibited from possessing a firearm under state law would be barred from permitless concealed carry protections. So individuals convicted of a misdemeanor act of domestic violence would be allowed under Ohio law to carry a concealed weapon without a permit.

Under the proposal, local law enforcement would be prohibited from working with federal entities on enforcement of firearms laws, a move that would limit the ability of police to get illegal guns off the streets and prosecute violent criminals.

City Attorney Klein also noted the striking similarity of HB 51’s draft language to nullification arguments used by slave states in the in the years preceding the Civil War.

In his testimony, City Attorney Klein wrote:

“HB 51 is an unconstitutional statute that will allow individuals who have been convicted of domestic violence to take advantage of the State’s permitless concealed carry law. It will destroy the ability of law enforcement agencies to work with their federal counterparts. It will open the State, its municipalities, and all of their employees up to endless litigation with the real threat of damages and attorneys’ fees. Finally, HB 51 embraces the discredited nullification language used by South Carolina and other states during the antebellum era.  This terrible bill should be rejected.”

Read City Attorney Klein’s full testimony HERE.

City Reaches Agreement for Safety Improvements at Hilltop Bar Plagued by Gun Violence

Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein recently announced that the City secured a preliminary injunction in the Franklin County Environmental Court ordering safety and security upgrades at Cain’s Sports Bar located in the Columbus Hilltop neighborhood. The bar was the scene of a double homicide where four individuals were shot in July 2022. In March 2023, three people were shot following a fight outside the bar around 2:30 a.m.

“Guns and alcohol are a bad mix that turn bar fights into deadly situations. With violence spilling out into the streets and threatening public safety, it was imperative that the City step in, hold bar owners accountable for this troubling behavior, and make sure they work with the experts at CPD and CFD to improve safety and security for patrons, employees and the surrounding neighborhood,” said Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein.

Under the terms of the agreed order, bar owners are shutting down operations earlier, hiring more security and allowing full police and fire security assessments to determine future safety and security plans to protect public safety.

“The City is willing to work with owners to improve security, but we won’t hesitate to take appropriate legal action if problems persist or owners are no longer cooperating. It’s a matter of public safety,” said Assistant City Attorney Sarah Pomeroy, the City’s chief attorney assigned to problem bars.

For a month following the signing of the order, bar owners have agreed to cease alcohol sales by 1:30 a.m. and close the premises by 2 a.m. The bar must also hire properly licensed security or off-duty Columbus police officers from 8 p.m. to 3 a.m. Thursday to Sunday and reassess security staffing levels one year following the signing of the order.

Additionally, CPD is now authorized to arrest and trespass all non-employees loitering after bar close. Bar owners must also submit to CPD and CFD security assessments of the property and operations.

“Neighbors in the Hilltop are rightly concerned about the levels of violence in and around this bar. While this agreement is a step forward, the City’s focus will remain on this bar to see that safety and security are a top priority—or we will take further action,” said Assistant City Attorney Zach Gwin, Zone attorney for the City’s west side neighborhoods, including the Hilltop.

City Files Amicus Brief in Case Challenging Legislature’s Attempt to Steal Power Away from Voters

Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein announced his office filed an amicus brief to the Ohio Supreme Court in One Person One Vote v. LaRose, a case challenging the legality of recently passed Senate Joint Resolution 2, which would create an August special election to put to the ballot a measure that would make it harder for Ohioans to pass constitutional amendments. Klein says the undemocratic measure is a direct response to a citizen-led effort to protect reproductive rights in Ohio. His statement is below:

“Ohio’s 1912 constitutional convention guaranteed power to the people through initiative and referendum to keep a check on the government. For more than a century, voters have taken this responsibility seriously, passing just 30 percent of all citizen-led initiatives since 1912.

“Now, less than a year after Statehouse Republicans passed legislation to limit the ability to hold August elections, these same politicians are singing a different tune the very first time they see the People rallying behind something they don’t like. Make no mistake, the timing of this isn’t coincidental. This is a Republican attempt to undercut the voters and change the rules because they don’t want to see reproductive rights on the ballot.

“If you care about reproductive rights and if you care about the ability of the People to hold their elected representatives in check, then you should care about this. There is no statutory basis for this election, and we urge the Court to grant the relief requested.”

Highlights from the City Attorney’s Office

Recently, Assistant City Attorney Sarah Pomeroy was awarded the prestigious Government in Action Award from the Ohio Women’s Bar Association for her continued work to improve the quality of life in Columbus by focusing on problem properties, nuisance bars and other businesses that attract crime and threaten public safety. Through her efforts as a member of the City Attorney’s Property Action Team, the City has shut down a record number of drug houses and dangerous businesses in recent years. As a dedicated and now highly-decorated public servant, the entire City Attorney’s Office congratulates Sarah for this well-deserved honor.

May 2023 - Addressing Gun Violence, Targeting Illegal Street Racing  & More

From the Desk of City Attorney Zach Klein

Gun violence and senseless tragedies have become all too common in neighborhoods across the city. But we cannot let them become the norm. No doubt, we are all concerned about the recent uptick in gun violence and I share those same concerns. In Linden, the Short North, the South Side, or elsewhere in our city, any instance of gun violence is unacceptable. Residents, business owners, workers and visitors deserve to feel safe and secure.

As city leaders, we must continue to be clear about what it takes to make our neighborhoods safe: police, prosecution, people, and the political will at the state and federal level to enact effective gun laws. Police need resources and additional personnel to deter crime and respond when it occurs, prosecutors and judges must prosecute violent and dangerous criminals to the fullest extent of the law, and people in our city need the support and opportunity to live a better life. And finally, we need Republican politicians at the state and federal level to find the courage to step up and pass effective, popularly-supported gun laws.

I hear these concerns from folks all across the city, and I couldn’t agree more. I’m angry and frustrated too. But we can’t give up. If we work together, we can save lives, improve public safety and continue to build a better, safer, stronger Columbus.

It is a privilege to serve as your City Attorney, and I will continue to listen to your thoughts and concerns on this and every other issue that matters most to you and your family. I encourage you to continue contacting our office at any time to let us know about what’s important to you. Please call 614.645.7385 or email CityAttorney@columbus.gov to share your thoughts on how we can better serve you.

City Attorney Klein Joins City Leaders to Urge Safe Storage of Firearms in Columbus Homes

City Attorney Klein recently joined Mayor Ginther, Police Chief Bryant and Public Health Director Roberts to urge gun owners to lock up their guns in their homes, in their cars, and everywhere they store their firearms. The call comes amid a rash of accidental shootings involving minors, including the City’s first test of its recently-passed safe storage law.

“There’s nothing wrong with responsible gun ownership, but leaving an unsecured gun around the house for kids to find is not responsible. That’s why it’s important that the City passed its safe storage law, and why we will continue to defend our right to enact commonsense measures to keep our kids and communities safe,” said City Attorney Zach Klein. “Too often, these incidents end in tragedy, but the fact is they are almost always preventable.”

During the call to action, Chief Bryant outlined several troubling cases where minors were able to gain access to dangerous firearms and discharge them and Dr. Roberts shared information on how responsible gun owners can obtain a lock box free of charge from the Department of Health by visiting www.columbus.gov/lockbox and filling out a request form. City leaders also urged gun owners to lock up or secure their firearms stored in their vehicles. The largest source of stolen guns in the United States are from parked cars, with an average of one gun stolen from a vehicle every 15 minutes nationally.

Additionally, City Attorney Klein detailed chilling video obtained depicting a child finding a loaded gun between couch cushions, pointing the weapon toward his head, and discharging the gun, narrowly missing his face. The video was key in the prosecution of the city’s first safe storage violation, where a Columbus man pleaded guilty to two counts of negligent storage of a firearm and one count of child endangerment in the incident caught on video.

“As a father, the images of a small child reaching into a couch cushion, finding a loaded firearm and discharging the weapon nearly pointed at his face are almost too chilling to watch,” said City Attorney Klein.

The defendant’s sentence was a joint recommendation after lengthy discussion with the mother of two of the juvenile victims in the case, and includes 10 days in jail, 170 days jail suspended, a $150 fine, two years of probation, and mandating that the firearm used in the incident be confiscated and destroyed. As part of the plea, the defendant must not own, possess or use a firearm for the duration of the probation period.

The case comes amid multiple lawsuits being pushed by the State of Ohio and the Buckeye Institute against the City’s recently passed gun safety ordinances, including measures to require safe storage of firearms in homes so that minors cannot access the weapons, limits on high capacity magazines, and steps to make it easier for prosecutors to go after individuals who sell firearms to those otherwise prohibited from owning or possessing a firearm, including those convicted of domestic violence.

City Officials Taking Action to Target Illegal Street Racing and Hold Offenders Accountable

City Attorney Klein recently joined Mayor Ginther and Police Chief Bryant to announce the City’s plans to ramp up enforcement and prosecution of illegal street racing and reckless operation of vehicles. City officials have received complaints from residents and business owners about street racing in multiple neighborhoods, and are taking action as this dangerous activity ramps up in the spring and summer months.

City Attorney Klein said that he has instructed city prosecutors to aggressively prosecute these offenders and hold them accountable for the danger they pose to public safety.

“Street racing is a real and immediate threat to public safety, and the City is responding in kind. We’re sending a message to anyone getting behind the wheel in Columbus: if you operate a vehicle recklessly, we will prosecute you,” said Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein. “During Operation Wheels Down, we impounded vehicles and aggressively prosecuted offenders. We’re going to do the same for drag racing—and make our streets safer in the process.”

On April 29, CPD responded to reports of street racing on the 4100 block of Indianola Ave. in Clintonville. Several spectators were also observed vandalizing vehicles in the area. When police arrived to disperse the scene, several gunshots were fired in the direction of the officers.

Earlier in April, one individual was killed in a crash believed to be connected to street racing in south Columbus. CPD is holding extensive planning and strategizing meetings with their officers to find additional ways to hold people accountable for their actions.

Enforcement and prosecution of reckless driving offenses have been a top priority for city leaders in recent years, with Columbus City Council passing an ordinance in 2021 enhancing penalties for illegal, reckless operation of certain vehicles on city streets.

In 2022, City Attorney Klein and Chief Bryant joined Columbus Mayor Andrew Ginther in unveiling Operation Wheels Down, a coordinated effort to step up enforcement and prosecution of individuals illegally and recklessly operating vehicles like dirt bikes and ATVs on city streets.

In the initial months of enforcement in 2022, Operation Wheels Down led to dozens of arrests and charges filed as well as the recovery of a number of stolen guns and vehicles. The City also impounded vehicles as evidence in many of these cases.

This joint announcement builds on the framework created under Operation Wheels Down as law enforcement and prosecutors work together to disrupt drag racing networks and events throughout the peak spring and summer months, impound offenders’ vehicles, and offer plea bargains only if there is an evidentiary issue that requires it. 

The City will also aggressively prosecute any other activity related to street racing such as weapon offenses, rioting, and property damage. Whenever legally permissible, the City will seize vehicles used to facilitate this conduct to the fullest extent allowed by law.

May 3 marked the one-year anniversary of the announcement of Operation Wheels Down.

City Attorney Zach Klein Announces Charges Filed in Softball Umpire Assault Case

City Attorney Klein recently announced multiple charges have been filed against a Columbus man accused of physically assaulting an adult recreational league softball umpire. City prosecutors charged the defendant with a first degree misdemeanor assault charge as well as a fourth degree disorderly conduct charge.

“The majority of sports officials aren’t in it for the money, but to give back to the sports they love. The assault on the umpire in Columbus is the nightmare scenario for any official and part of the larger problem of why we continue to see a decline in sports officials both locally and across the country. Threats and violence have no place in sports or in our community,” said Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein, who has spent over 20 years as a basketball referee beginning as an intramural referee in college and working at all levels of basketball, most recently as an NCAA Division-I Women’s Basketball official.

The assault occurred during a Columbus Recreation and Parks Department adult slowpitch softball league at Lou Berliner Sports Complex, where the defendant struck the umpire in the face following the defendant’s ejection from the game for arguing.

Members of the opposing team rushed to aid the umpire, pulling the defendant away from the victim. No other individuals were involved in the incident and no additional charges have been filed at this time.

Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein Opposes Changes that would make it Harder for Citizens to Pass Constitutional Amendments

City Attorney Klein issued a statement in opposition to efforts by Statehouse Republican lawmakers to pass a constitutional amendment that would make it harder for citizens to pass any future amendments to the Ohio Constitution by removing majority rule and replacing it with a 60 percent passage threshold.

“This amendment is an undemocratic, unpopular and unfair power grab by extremist politicians and the special interests that bankroll their campaigns. This proposal would get rid of citizen-led ballot initiatives as we know them by stripping away the ability for the majority of voters to decide what’s best for our state. 

“The truth is that Ohioans already understand the gravity of what it means to amend our constitution. That’s why voters have opposed more than 70 percent of citizen-initiated constitutional amendments since 1912. Time and again Ohioans have shown they take their voting responsibility seriously, and yet, the entire basis of this proposal is that voters can’t be trusted. I reject that notion. When the majority of Ohioans speak, politicians should listen. We need to trust the voters, not limit their voice and their power. This amendment must be rejected.”

City Attorney Zach Klein Files Lawsuit as City Shuts Down Illegal After-Hours Club

City Attorney Klein announced his office has filed a lawsuit against the operators of an illegal after-hours club located at 2400 East Dublin Granville Road. Columbus Police executed a search warrant at the club around 1:30 a.m. on Saturday, April 15, where officers charged individuals and seized property associated with the illegal operation, including liquor and music equipment.

“We’ve seen increased crime and violence emanating from illegal after-hours clubs across the city, and now is the time to crack down on operators who skirt liquor laws, ignore occupancy and safety codes, and overlook violence spilling out into the community,” said Columbus City Attorney Zach Klein. “If a bar, club or any business threatens public safety, we’ll use every legal tool we have to hold owners accountable. The City is sending a clear message: you can’t set up illegal clubs and expect to operate under your own set of rules. We’ll shut you down.”

The City is currently investigating several potential connections between the illegal East Dublin Granville Road operation and an illegal after-hours club in south Franklinton that the City shut down in March 2023. That club, known as “The Underground,” had been the scene of violence and criminal activity, as well as numerous safety code violations, including overcrowding and locked entry/exit points. That property was also connected to a double homicide that occurred just blocks from the premises in the week leading up to the City shutting it down.
